skill.name: Why this device here? Mood and effect
skill.why: Writers pick each picture on purpose. It sets how the scene feels.
skill.how: Find the picture. Ask how it makes you feel. Check the rest of the passage agrees.

steps.say: My spooky story starts here. Picture it.
steps.ask: How does that picture make you feel?

options.text: cosy
options.reason: Would a cold, wet hand on your neck feel cosy?

options.text: creepy
excited
options.reason: Picture a cold, wet hand reaching for you. Is that fun?

steps.win: Yes, creepy! How a place feels is called its mood.

steps.say: Now watch. Same fog, different picture.

options.text: scary
options.reason: Is a soft blanket scary? Picture snuggling into one.

options.text: angry
options.reason: Nobody is cross. What's a soft blanket like?

options.text: cosy

steps.win: Yes! Swap the picture, and the whole mood changes.

steps.say: A picture can be a simile, metaphor or personification.

encounters.frame: The Moodgill found Wren's night diary on the boardwalk. Its fins have gone grey.
encounters.text: Night fell over the mangroves. Wren walked the boardwalk alone. The water was black and still. Her torch flickered. The roots stuck out of the mud like bony fingers. Something splashed. The mist curled around her ankles. Wren walked faster. Then her torch went out. Somewhere behind her, a branch snapped. She did not look back. She ran all the way to the boat.
encounters.prompt: Why did the writer say the roots were 'like bony fingers'?
encounters.success: Creepy. Bony fingers reaching out of the mud fit a dark night that sends Wren running.

options.text: to make the mangroves feel friendly
options.reason: Bony fingers poking out of mud aren't friendly. Wren ends up running away.

options.text: to make the mangroves feel creepy
to make the mangroves feel funny
options.reason: Nothing here is a joke. Wren runs to the boat without looking back.

encounters.frame: A space log has drifted into the mangroves. The Moodgill is reading it by moonlight.
encounters.text: Captain Lin's radio broke three days ago. Since then, nobody had spoken to her. She floated by the window of her little ship. Outside, the stars stared back like cold, silent eyes. Earth was a blue speck, as small as a crumb. She waved at it anyway. She whispered, 'Goodnight, everyone.' Nobody answered. She hugged her pillow and closed her eyes.

options.reason: Nothing here is a joke. Lin hugs her pillow because she is alone.

encounters.frame: Indi posted a letter home from Mirage Mangroves. The Moodgill's fins are glowing gold.
encounters.text: Dear Nan, today Mo and I went snorkelling off the edge of the mangroves. I was nervous at first, because the water near the roots looked dark. Then we swam out past the last tree, and everything changed. The water was as clear as a just-washed window. Little fish burst out of the coral like confetti thrown at a party, orange and yellow and electric blue. A turtle cruised past us, slow and smooth. Mo laughed so hard into his snorkel that he swallowed half the sea. I didn't want to get out, even when my fingers went wrinkly. Tomorrow we're going back with a camera. Love, Indi
encounters.prompt: Why does Indi say the fish burst out 'like confetti thrown at a party'?
encounters.success: Joyful. Confetti means a party, and Indi laughs, stays in the water and plans to come back.

options.text: to make the reef feel tense and dangerous
options.reason: Her nerves come before the confetti fish. Confetti is for parties, not danger.

options.text: to make the reef feel bright and joyful
to make the reef feel dull and empty
options.reason: Confetti is colourful and fills the air. Does that sound dull?

encounters.frame: Zed has posted a game review on the crew noticeboard. The Moodgill read it twice.
encounters.text: Zed's game review: Castle Shadowfang, Level 9. This is the hardest level I have ever played. You sneak through a castle with only three lives left. The music starts slowly, like a heartbeat, then gets faster and faster the closer you get to the boss. Every door might hide a trap. The walls creak. Your torch flickers. Twice, I paused the game just to breathe. My hands were so sweaty that the controller nearly slipped. When the boss finally appeared, I screamed so loudly that Mum came running. She thought something had bitten me. Score: ten out of ten. Would never play again.
encounters.prompt: Why does Zed compare the music to a heartbeat that gets faster?
encounters.success: Tense. Your heartbeat races when you're scared, so the music makes every step feel risky.

options.reason: A racing heartbeat isn't calm. Zed has to pause the game just to breathe.

options.reason: Nothing sad happens. Zed is on the edge of his seat, not unhappy.

options.text: to make the level feel tense

encounters.frame: Tully wrote up the Mangrove Paddle Race for the island newsletter. The Moodgill's fins went gold, then grey.
encounters.text: The Mangrove Paddle Race started on a perfect morning. The channel glittered like a tray of sequins, and the crew's canoe slid along so smoothly that Tully started singing the Reef Rays club song. Mo trailed his fingers in the warm water and said this was the best race ever. Behind them, the other canoes were tiny dots, and Zed was already practising his winner's speech. By lunchtime they were in the lead. Then Zed pointed behind them. A purple cloud was creeping over the treetops like a bruise spreading across the sky. The birds stopped calling. The wind dropped, then came back cold and sudden, slapping little waves against the canoe. Tully stopped singing. 'Paddle,' she said quietly. 'Paddle now.' The first fat drops hit the water like flicked stones. They reached the finish line just as the thunder cracked. They came second, soaked to the bone, and nobody cared about the ribbon.
encounters.prompt: Why does the writer describe the cloud as 'like a bruise spreading across the sky'?
encounters.success: A spreading bruise is dark and painful, so the cloud warns that the sunny race is turning dangerous.

options.text: to show the race is getting calmer and easier
options.reason: Things get harder, not easier. The wind turns cold and Tully stops singing.

options.text: to show that someone in the canoe has been hurt
options.reason: Nobody is hurt. The bruise describes the cloud's purple colour and how it spreads.

options.text: to show the perfect morning is turning threatening
to show the crew is bored of being in the lead
options.reason: Nobody is bored. Straight after the cloud, Tully tells everyone to paddle now.

encounters.frame: Gus wrote a note about a story called 'Unit Seven'. One word is wrong.
encounters.text: Unit Seven was the last robot left in the old toy factory. Everyone else had gone home years ago, and the machines had been switched off one by one. Every morning, Unit Seven still swept the floor and said 'Good morning' to the empty desks. Nobody ever said it back. Its beeps echoed like a ball bounced in an empty hall. The dust on the shelves was a grey blanket nobody wanted. The clock on the wall had given up at ten past three, and nobody had come to fix it. Sometimes it built a little wooden duck, set it on a desk, and waited for someone to say thank you. Nobody did. One night, a possum crept in through a broken window. Unit Seven froze, then slowly held out a wooden duck. The possum sniffed it, took it, and came back the next night. After that, Unit Seven started making two ducks a day.

encounters.frame: Sami wrote about Sundays for the class anthology. The Moodgill curled up on the page.
encounters.text: Every Sunday, Sami caught the bus to her nonna's flat above the bakery. The stairs up to the flat always smelled of fresh bread. The moment she opened the door, the kitchen smelled like a hug. Pots of sauce bubbled on the stove, and a loaf of bread sat cooling on the bench, its crust crackling like a tiny campfire. Nonna would be humming an old song, with flour on her nose, and she would pinch Sami's cheeks as if she had not seen her for a year. They rolled gnocchi together at the little table by the window. Sami's were always lumpy, but Nonna said lumpy ones held more sauce. Afterwards they ate in the sunny corner, and Nonna told the same story about the goat that ate her wedding hat. Sami had heard it fifty times. She laughed anyway, every single time. On the bus home, her pockets were always full of biscuits wrapped in paper napkins.
encounters.prompt: 'The kitchen smelled like a hug.' Which other detail shows the place is loving, not just warm?
encounters.success: Pinching cheeks as if it had been a year shows Nonna loves Sami. Bread and sauce are only warm.

options.reason: A campfire is warm and cosy, but it's about bread. It doesn't show anyone's love.

options.reason: Bubbling sauce is warm food, but it doesn't show how Nonna feels about Sami.

options.text: Nonna pinched Sami's cheeks as if it had been a year.
The stairs up to the flat always smelled of fresh bread.
options.reason: A lovely smell, but it is on the stairs. It shows nothing about Nonna and Sami.

encounters.frame: Indi left her sketchbook open on deck. The Moodgill read her notes and went very grey.
encounters.text: Nobody had used the old jetty at Crooked Creek for thirty years. At dusk, Zed and Indi rowed out to sketch it. Indi wanted to draw the broken boathouse, and Zed wanted to prove he wasn't scared. The water was still, like a held breath. The posts leaned out of the mud like tired old men who had forgotten why they were standing there. A rusty bell hung at the end, and every so often it gave one soft clang, though there was no wind at all. Indi's pencil stopped moving. 'Did you see that?' she whispered. A light flickered in the boathouse window, pale as a moth, then went out. Zed suddenly remembered that he had left the kettle on, back on the boat, and that they should go and check it. Right now. They rowed home faster than they had ever rowed. Neither of them mentioned that the boat didn't have a kettle.
encounters.prompt: Which explanation of the writer's pictures fits this passage?
encounters.success: A held breath means waiting for something to happen, which suits a bell that rings without wind.

options.text: 'Like tired old men' shows that Zed is tired after rowing.
options.reason: The picture is about the posts, not Zed. Mood is how the whole place feels.

options.text: 'Pale as a moth' makes the light feel warm and safe.
options.reason: A pale light flickering in an empty boathouse isn't safe. Zed and Indi flee.

options.text: 'Like a held breath' makes the creek feel lazy and relaxed.
options.reason: Holding your breath isn't relaxed. You do it while you wait, nervous, for something.

options.text: 'Like a held breath' makes the creek feel tense and waiting.

encounters.frame: Indi found this story pinned to the bakery noticeboard on Harbour Lane. The Moodgill's fins went from grey to gold.
encounters.text: Rain had been falling on Harbour Lane since breakfast, and by four o'clock the whole street looked like a photo left out in the sun to fade. Umbrellas hurried past with their heads down. Shop windows fogged over. A busker stood under the bakery awning with a battered violin case open at his feet, holding three coins and a bus ticket. Nobody looked at him. A delivery van splashed through a puddle and soaked his shoes. For a while he just tuned his strings, as if he wasn't sure anyone wanted to hear. Then he began to play. The music spilled out like warm light from an open door. A woman with a pram slowed down. A man in a soggy suit stopped checking his phone. A little boy in a yellow raincoat let go of his dad's hand and started stomping in a puddle, perfectly in time, sending up splashes that glittered under the streetlights. The baker came out, wiping her hands on her apron, and leaned in the doorway to listen. When the song ended, people clapped with wet hands and dropped coins into the case until it rattled. The rain hadn't stopped. Somehow, nobody seemed to mind anymore. The busker played until the streetlights came on.
encounters.prompt: The writer could have written 'The music was lovely.' What does 'spilled out like warm light from an open door' do that 'lovely' can't?
encounters.success: The street is grey, wet and cold. The music brings the warm light it lacks, and people gather.

options.text: It gives the grey, rainy street the warmth and light it was missing.
It shows the bakery door was open, so its warm light spilled onto the street.
options.reason: That reads it as really true. The open door is a picture of how the music feels.

options.text: It tells the reader the music poured out loudly and flooded the whole street.
options.reason: Light doesn't tell you how loud something is. It's about warmth on a grey, cold day.

options.text: It shows the busker's nerves fading, like a door slowly opening.
options.reason: He tunes as if unsure, but this picture is about the music, not his nerves.

encounters.frame: Zed wrote about the crew's fishing trip off Mirage Point. The Moodgill refused to get in the boat.
encounters.prompt: Tap the picture where the mood turns.
encounters.success: A box nobody should open hides something you don't want to meet. Then fish, gulls and crew pull away.

parts: On the morning the crew went fishing off Mirage Point, everything seemed perfect.

parts.tap: Sunlight danced and winked on the waves, like a thousand tiny mirrors playing a game.
parts.reason: Dancing, winking sunlight is bright and playful. The morning still feels cheerful.

parts: Tully had packed enough sandwiches for a week, and Mo had brought a bucket of his famous sardine bait, which smelled exactly as bad as it sounds. Zed had brought his lucky cap, which had never once been lucky.

parts.tap: The esky lid squeaked open like a happy puppy that wanted to come fishing too.
parts.reason: A happy puppy is cheerful and friendly. The trip still feels fun here.

parts: They dropped anchor where the reef ended.

parts.tap: The anchor chain rattled down into the deep, like coins tumbling into a money box.
parts.reason: The deep sounds risky, but coins in a money box are a happy sound. Nothing has turned yet.

parts.tap: Mo's floppy hat was a seagull trying to escape, flapping and tugging in the breeze.
parts.reason: Trying to escape sounds worried, but a hat-seagull is a joke. The mood is still light.

parts: For an hour, nobody caught anything except sunburn. Then Zed leaned over the side to rinse his hands.

parts.tap: Below the boat, the water was a dark, smooth lid on a box that nobody should open.

parts: He pulled his hands back without quite knowing why. The fishing lines hung straight down, perfectly still, and not a single fish nibbled. Even the gulls, which had followed them all morning hoping for sardines, had drifted away towards the shore. Tully checked the sky, which was blue from edge to edge. 'Probably nothing,' she said. Mo began reeling in his line, very slowly, and suggested that the sandwiches might taste better back at the mangroves. Nobody argued.

encounters.frame: Zed is rewriting his guide to his favourite game. The Moodgill is reading the new draft over his shoulder.
encounters.text: LEVEL 7: THE FROST PLAINS. Zed is rewriting his guide to Skyquest, the game he plays every arvo. The Frost Plains are the quietest level in the game. There are no shops, no music and no other players, and your map shows nothing for miles. In his first draft, Zed wrote: 'An old lighthouse stands by the sea.' Indi read it and shrugged. 'That just tells me what's there,' she said. 'It doesn't make me feel anything.' So Zed tried again. His new line reads: 'A ruined lighthouse leans over the frozen sea, still waiting for a ship that never came.' After it, he added: 'A single crow sits on a fence post, and nobody comes to meet it.' Indi read the new version twice. Then she went quiet for a while, which Zed decided was a very good sign. Mo, who had been reading over her shoulder, said it made him want to give the lighthouse a hug. Zed has now rewritten six levels this way, and he says the Frost Plains took the longest.
encounters.prompt: What does Zed's new lighthouse line do that his first draft didn't?
encounters.success: 'Still waiting for a ship that never came' gives the lighthouse a sad wait, so the plains feel forgotten.

options.text: It makes the lighthouse seem ready to strike, so the level feels dangerous and tense.
options.reason: Leaning and waiting for a ship is not getting ready to attack. Nothing in the line threatens the player.

options.text: It promises that a ship is coming soon, so the level feels hopeful and exciting.
options.reason: 'A ship that never came' says no ship arrives. There's nothing left to hope for.

options.text: It makes the lighthouse seem forgotten, so the whole level feels empty and lonely.
It describes the lighthouse in more detail, so players can find it on their map.
options.reason: The map shows nothing for miles. The new words add a feeling, not directions.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote a note about Indi's mural for the Pelican Flat newsletter. One word is wrong.
encounters.text: When the floodwater finally drained out of Pelican Flat, it left behind a town the colour of old tea. Mud coated the footpaths, the playground and the bottom half of every shop window. Fences lay flat, as if a giant had sat on them. For two weeks, people shovelled, scrubbed and carried ruined couches out to the kerb, hardly speaking. The air smelled of wet carpet and river mud, and even the cockatoos had lost their voices. Indi was asked to paint a mural on the side of the town hall, the only wall that had stayed dry. She wasn't sure what to paint. A celebration felt wrong while half the town was still sleeping in the school gym. So she painted what she could see from the hall steps at dawn: the muddy paddocks, the broken fence posts, the crooked gum tree with a kayak still stuck in its branches. And above all of it, she painted the sun rising over the drowned paddocks like a promise someone meant to keep. On the morning the mural was finished, an old farmer stood in front of it for a long time with his hat in his hands. Then he went home and started rebuilding his fence. By the end of the week, three more fences were going up along the same road.
encounters.prompt: Tap the word Wren got wrong, then choose a better one.
encounters.success: Hopeful. Nothing is won yet, so it isn't triumphant. A promise someone means to keep says better days are coming.

parts: The sun rising 'like a promise someone meant to keep' makes the mural feel

parts.tap: triumphant

parts: . Fences flat 'as if a giant had sat on them' make the damage seem

parts.tap: huge
parts.reason: Only something giant could squash every fence flat. Huge fits.

parts: . Cockatoos that 'had lost their voices' make the town seem

parts.tap: hushed and sad
parts.reason: When even noisy birds lose their voices, the whole town has gone quiet. That fits.

options.text: frightening
options.reason: A promise someone means to keep is a good thing. Nothing in the mural is a threat.

options.text: carefree
options.reason: The town has just flooded. People are working hard and hardly speaking.

options.text: hopeful
furious
options.reason: Nobody is angry at anyone. The farmer stands quietly, then goes home to rebuild.

encounters.frame: The crew is watching Maxx Vantablack's latest live stream from Green Screen Swamp. The Moodgill has a front-row seat.
encounters.text: 'Maxx it out, Vantafam!' The MaxxCam drone swooped low over Green Screen Swamp as Maxx Vantablack stepped off his gold jet ski. Two Goldies in gold tracksuits rolled out a gold carpet across the mud, which sank almost immediately. According to his own live commentary, he strode onto the riverbank like a king arriving at his coronation, sunlight blazing off his silver hair, his brand-new gold gumboots gleaming like trophies. 'Today,' he announced, spreading his arms wide, 'I rescue the rarest Creature in the mangroves, with my bare hands.' He took one magnificent step forward. The mud took his left boot. He took another step. The mud took his right boot. For a moment he stood perfectly still in his gold socks, still smiling at the drone, while a fiddler crab strolled across his toes. Then he slowly tipped backwards into the swamp, with a sound like a giant slurping the last of a milkshake. The drone kept filming. Somewhere, millions of Vantafam watched the bubbles rise. Up in the mangroves, the Moodgill made a noise that sounded suspiciously like laughing. 'That's Maxx-imum content!' gurgled Maxx, from somewhere under the mud. 'Stay gold!' The Goldies looked at each other, then went to find a very long stick.
encounters.prompt: Why does the writer describe Maxx arriving 'like a king arriving at his coronation'?
encounters.success: The grander Maxx looks going in, the funnier it is when the mud swallows his boots and then him.

options.text: to make readers feel truly sorry for Maxx when he falls
options.reason: He isn't hurt, and the passage plays it for laughs. Even the Moodgill is laughing.

options.text: to show that Maxx is a quiet and humble person
options.reason: A king arriving to be crowned is grand, not humble. Maxx announces himself to millions.

options.text: to warn readers that the swamp is a deadly place
options.reason: The coronation picture is about Maxx, not the swamp. Nothing deadly happens. He just gets muddy.

options.text: to puff Maxx up so that his muddy fall is funnier

encounters.frame: Gus has written up Experiment 47 for the Field Guide. The Moodgill has buried itself in the mud.
encounters.prompt: Gus promised Experiment 47 was completely safe. Tap the picture that tells the reader not to believe him.
encounters.success: A slime that is hungry, just awake and feeling its way to food is alive. That personification makes it menacing.

parts: Gus called it Experiment 47, and he had promised the crew it was completely safe. He had said the same about Experiments 1 to 46, and most of those had ended with the fire extinguisher.

parts.tap: The lab was a dentist's waiting room, with every jar labelled and every spoon in a row.
parts.reason: A tidy waiting room is calm and orderly. It makes the lab look safe, not dangerous.

parts: He tipped a spoonful of green powder into a bucket of swamp water and stirred. At first, nothing happened. Then the mixture began to bubble, and a smell like a thousand forgotten lunchboxes rolled across the room. Mo gagged.

parts.tap: Gus hummed, as happy as a kid in a lolly shop.
parts.reason: A kid in a lolly shop is cheerful. It shows Gus isn't worried at all.

parts: The slime rose over the rim of the bucket.

parts.tap: It crept across the bench, hungry and just awake, feeling its way towards Gus's sandwich.

parts: Gus took a careful step back. 'Interesting,' he said, in a voice that was trying hard to sound calm.

parts.tap: Outside the porthole, the sunset glowed like a bowl of warm peaches.
parts.reason: Warm peaches make the sunset gentle and sweet. They say nothing about danger.

parts: The slime reached the sandwich and swallowed it with a soft, satisfied gloop. Then it turned, very slowly, towards the crew. 'That's not gross,' whispered Gus. 'That's science.' Nobody stayed to argue. The Moodgill stayed in the mud until dinner. Later, Gus wrote one word in his notebook: SUCCESS.
